status: Work paused at the agreed stopping point. Strict 60 FPS is still open.
summary: The final clean build delivered 58.55 frames/s containing new samples over 75 seconds. An earlier run reached 61.25. Both started with 10M samples across ten series and acquired 100 samples every 10 ms. That is close enough for this iteration, but I would not call 60 FPS reliable yet. The results require a fixed overview and the settings listed below.
findings: The final build kept 10,749,900 samples and delivered 58.55 new-data FPS. Frame intervals were 23.83 ms p95, 37.53 ms p99 and 115.63 ms at worst. Measurement averaged 2.57 ms and drawing 2.94 ms. The earlier 75-second run reached 61.25 new-data FPS, with 19.84 ms p95 and 28.94 ms p99 intervals. The final build removes temporary tracing and sets dark tooltip text on a light background.

The final run held mean frame intervals near 16.0 to 16.5 ms for its first 60 seconds, then slowed down. It allocated 1.787 GB and recorded 1,142 ms of GC pauses over the whole run. We have not established what caused the late slowdown. Storage growth happened earlier, while frame intervals stayed close to their previous level.

Ordinary lines were already too slow at ten series of 1,000 samples each. The controlled baseline took 125.70 ms per update, draw and tooltip query. Removing markers, fills, smoothing and point animation reduced that to 57.10 ms. At ten series of 10,000 samples, even the stripped version took 334.74 ms.

Reducing the data before rendering helped, but ordinary line objects still cost too much. At 10M retained samples, indexed representatives passed through ordinary lines took 224.40 ms per iteration. The first streaming renderer took 49.10 ms. Its main costs were measurement at 30.50 ms and drawing at 18.49 ms. Nearest-X lookup took 0.087 ms.

Caching extrema values reduced median full-view selection time from 4.59 to 2.94 ms for one source of 10M samples. Managed memory rose from 241.1 to 261.2 MiB. A separate comparison of 32-sample and 8-sample index blocks cut median selection time from 1.481 to 1.024 ms, at a further memory cost of 357.2 MiB. The smaller blocks are a deliberate speed/memory tradeoff. Bit-mask traversal also had promising results, but timing varied between repetitions. The raw runs are retained below.

The append cache avoided full selection in all three measurement profiles. Each run recorded 3,000 tail selections and no full selections. Path rebuilding still took 71 to 76% of measurement time. Caching unchanged pixel coordinates addressed that cost. Three paired runs improved from 5.867 to 1.728 ms, 5.337 to 1.736 ms, and 5.781 to 1.524 ms. Candidate p95 was 2.12 to 2.85 ms.

Stroke width mattered far more than expected. In the isolated raster test, an antialiased one-unit path took 7.33 ms at 100% scaling and 155.79 ms at 125%. A 0.8-unit stroke at 125%, one physical pixel, took 13.28 ms. UseOnePixelStroke makes that appearance change explicit. It does not change Windows display settings.

The CPU raster cache cut mean Avalonia drawing time from 28.32 to 7.62 ms in the first matched fixed-view runs. Total drawing rate rose from 20.16 to 34.50 FPS. Caching selected coordinates later produced fixed-view trials of 46.19 and 52.52 FPS. Those single runs show the direction of progress, but laptop timing varied too much to treat every difference as a precise speedup.

Two faster drawing experiments were not adopted. Min/max rectangles took 6.51 to 8.51 ms but changed the line shape and showed seams at fractional scaling. Bulk AddPoly construction saved roughly 0.41 ms for ten precomputed paths. That saving was real, but too small to explain the much larger chart measurement cost.

A short synchronous-update trial appeared to reach 59.95 FPS, but it contained only 588 measurements for 901 draws. Animation-only draws inflated the apparent update rate. The benchmark now counts frames containing new samples separately. Earlier 75-second variants reached only 49.45 and 35.33 FPS, so they were not evidence of sustained 60 FPS.

Tooltips have a measurable cost beyond looking up a sample. Removing pointer and query work reduced drawing from 7.22 to 3.59 ms in one paired trial. The application still fell below 50 new-data FPS. The later EventPipe capture recorded 1,988 allocation samples with stacks and no lost events. Axis label measurement accounted for at least 40.2% of weighted allocation; tooltip code accounted for at least 11.7%. These are lower bounds from the top 80 stacks, and nested operations overlap.

Reusing a temporary axis label geometry reduced allocation per measurement by 32.1%, from 309,293 to 210,141 bytes. The controlled CPU comparison measured 1.00 and 1.22 ms for the baseline, versus 0.88 and 0.94 ms for the change. Avalonia confirmed lower allocation, but its paired FPS results overlapped. I would keep this change for its allocation savings. The UI runs do not establish an FPS increase.

The tooltip shadow was the clearest remaining drawing cost. With identical explicit paints apart from the shadow filter, drawing fell from 7.39 to 3.36 ms when the shadow was removed. New-data FPS rose from 51.45 to 56.87 in that short pair. Text, layout, pointer following and animation remained enabled. The final configuration also sets the text color explicitly so it stays readable.

The frame trace did not support changing dispatcher priority. Background invalidation dispatch stayed below 1 ms at p95. Removing the shadow reduced full custom drawing from 9.93 to 4.87 ms and intervals over 25 ms from 117/508 to 4/624. Inspection of Avalonia 12.0.1 also ruled out a deliberate 16 ms sleep after each draw. Its timer is periodic. The temporary trace hooks have been removed, with patches saved for reproduction.

The fixed overview is the strongest result. Earlier moving-view trials reached 25.97 new-data FPS; an automatically expanding overview reached 24.08. Those trials still allowed automatic updates alongside the explicit publisher. We have not repeated them with the final manual-update configuration. Do not apply the fixed-view result to those modes.
changes: TimeSeriesBuffer retains the original models, converts X/Y once at append, indexes extrema and finds the nearest timestamp without scanning the full history.

StreamingLineSeries uses the existing render override. It draws selected samples in one path per series, reuses unchanged pixel coordinates and can cache CPU-rendered pixels. Ordinary series keep their existing rendering path.

UpdateSynchronously lets an application that owns the UI frame callback invoke measurement without the worker-to-UI scheduling round trip. The caller supplies pacing. Existing rendering-activity checks can still skip a measurement until another draw begins.

Axis sizing reuses one temporary geometry per call and releases its native text resources after each label. Formatter and font-builder calls stay unchanged. Empty labels now clear their previous cached text.
Chart unload releases per-view render resources under the canvas lock. Theme changes and image exports use the guarded update path, so callbacks cannot recursively measure the chart.

The benchmark tools now cover retained CPU updates, source queries, path construction, software rasterization, real Avalonia updates and allocation sampling. They save JSON results. The older image-export benchmarks are described as exports rather than retained updates.
validation: The final full .NET 8 suite passed 868 of 870 tests. The two failures are pre-existing decimal-dot and US-currency expectations on this German-culture machine. The final focused run passed 27 of 27 tests.

The clean Avalonia build and production builds for .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Framework 4.6.2 passed. git diff --check found no whitespace errors. The SDK test orchestration failed earlier, so validation used an explicit Release build and the built MSTest executable.

Source tests compare selection and bounds against a brute-force reference. Cases include chunk and tree boundaries, duplicate timestamps, missing data, reset, mapping identity and extreme finite timestamps.

Renderer tests cover bounded representative counts, original-model tooltips, gaps, appends, resets, pan, zoom, resize, inverse X, viewport animation and cached-versus-fresh output. Lifecycle tests cover shared series, unloading, reloading and collection of detached views.

All 15 raster-cache image cases passed on Avalonia Skia 3.119. Cached output differed by at most 1/255 per channel. The Core Skia 2.88 integration cases showed differences up to 4/255. Unsupported blending used the direct drawing fallback. These tolerances describe the observed pixels, not a claim of exact equivalence.

The axis tests check empty text, formatter calls, changed fonts, rotation, padding, shared paints, cleanup after exceptions and repeated disposal. The synchronous-update tests cover reentrancy and the production rendering-activity guard.

Avalonia MCP connected to a separate diagnostic run. Its visual tree contained the chart and motion canvas. Screenshots showed ten dense series and the complete ten-row tooltip without clipping. That screenshot uses the earlier default tooltip style. The corrected final colors are explicit in code; the final MCP capture did not complete before work stopped.

Both long trials used a visible, unminimized window. Each produced 7,500 batches, appended 7,499 and left one queued at shutdown. The report keeps that final queued batch separate from samples counted as displayed.
No benchmark or diagnostic process from this work remains running.
limitations: The numbers measure chart drawing. We did not measure physical monitor presents. Pointer movement is synthetic and exercises the real tooltip layout and drawing code, but does not measure operating-system mouse latency.

Early Avalonia runs appended without Canvas.Sync. Render-time viewport refinement can read the same source, so those results remain exploratory. The final benchmark locks source updates and reports lock wait.
The source is append-only and the caller owns synchronization. It has no rolling retention, historical editing or automatic detection of changes to existing models.
The long trials lasted 75 to 90 seconds after preloading 10M samples. We did not run a multi-hour soak. Memory continues to grow as samples arrive.

Reduction preserves selected extrema and sample identity but loses subpixel detail. It prevents connections across detected gaps without preserving every tiny segment. A one-sample line has no visible marker.

The machine was not isolated from other desktop work. JIT compilation, CPU frequency and scheduling may affect the results. We did not measure those factors well enough to name the cause of the final slowdown.
The CPU benchmark uses SkiaSharp 2.88.9. The Avalonia application uses 3.119.3-preview.1.1. Compare variants within each benchmark; their absolute drawing costs come from different Skia versions.
